title: Four Traits of Rockstar Teacher Teams
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. borrows from Tracy Kidder's The Soul of a New Machine to ask what makes teams both purposeful and enjoyable. He identifies four conditions: a difficult task, a clear and compelling goal, personal responsibility for each member, and individual freedom in pursuit of the work. He says these are rare in school teams and illustrates them with a hypothetical team charged with measuring and improving the eighth-to-ninth grade transition. Each teacher gets a real, distinct piece of the problem rather than a token contribution. He insists that freedom means decluttering, so joining the team should mean dropping other commitments. He ends by inviting readers to consider the connections and the possible unintended consequences.
points: Great teams share four conditions: a hard task, a compelling goal, personal responsibility and individual freedom.
The ninth-grade transition example turns an abstract ideal into a concrete team charge with measurable pieces.
Responsibility must be substantive, with each teacher owning a distinct problem, not contributing a slide for a report.
Freedom for teachers largely means permission to stop doing other things, so team membership cannot be one more add-on.
Stuart models learning leadership lessons from a non-education book, with a candid question about unintended consequences.
quotes: But nonetheless, Kidder’s book has much to teach us, particularly when it comes to the conditions that make great teams great. Consider how much fun it would be — how professionally developing, how long-term-flourishing-centric — to be on a team where all of the following were true:
I’ve found these four traits to be rare in school-based teams. Let’s use a hypothetical example from my own school to illustrate these four conditions.

Here would be a challenging task: How do we measure and improve the strength of the transition to high school for all kids, as simply (i.e., without increasing staffing) as possible? Then, frame the task with a clear and compelling goal.
Teacher B, we need you to find the easiest way to measure connection to school. We know that we want kids to get “plugged in” and have a community.
Teacher E, you want to be an administrator someday. Awesome. That’s going to require navigating conflicting pressures on your time and leading people who also have to do this navigation work.

Participation on this team should mean non-participation on others. Otherwise, team participation feels like just one more thing. There’s no signal that this team is important if we don’t declutter their path a bit.
